name: VM-Based Legacy
description: A pattern for hosting applications on virtual machines when containerisation or serverless is not feasible. Common for legacy applications that require specific OS configurations, commercial software with licensing constraints, or workloads being lifted-and-shifted to cloud as a first migration step.
whenToUse: Legacy applications that cannot be containerised without significant refactoring
Commercial software with licensing models tied to specific OS or VM configurations
Lift-and-shift cloud migration as a first step before modernisation
Applications requiring specific OS-level configurations or kernel modules
Workloads with regulatory requirements mandating dedicated compute instances
whenNotToUse: New application development where containers or serverless would be more appropriate
Stateless web applications that could benefit from managed platform services
Workloads with highly variable traffic that need rapid auto-scaling
Applications where the team has container expertise and the app is container-ready
Simple workloads where the operational overhead of VM management is disproportionate

typicalComponents.name: Virtual Machines
typicalComponents.purpose: Host application workloads on dedicated compute instances
typicalComponents.technology: EC2, Azure VMs, or Compute Engine

typicalComponents.name: Load Balancer
typicalComponents.purpose: Distribute traffic across multiple VM instances for availability
typicalComponents.technology: ALB/NLB, Azure Load Balancer, or Cloud Load Balancing

typicalComponents.name: Configuration Management
typicalComponents.purpose: Automate OS configuration, patching, and software installation
typicalComponents.technology: Ansible, Puppet, Chef, or AWS Systems Manager

typicalComponents.name: Backup Service
typicalComponents.purpose: Automated VM snapshots and data backup with retention policies
typicalComponents.technology: AWS Backup, Azure Backup, or Cloud Backup

typicalComponents.name: Monitoring Agent
typicalComponents.purpose: Collect OS and application metrics from VM instances
typicalComponents.technology: CloudWatch Agent, Azure Monitor Agent, or Ops Agent

securityControls: Implement automated OS patching on a defined schedule with compliance reporting
Harden VM images using CIS benchmarks or NCSC guidance
Restrict network access using security groups and network ACLs
Implement endpoint detection and response (EDR) agents on all VMs
Disable unnecessary services and ports on VM instances
Implement privileged access management for SSH/RDP access to VMs
Encrypt VM disks at rest using platform-managed or customer-managed keys
resilienceConsiderations: Deploy VMs across multiple availability zones with load balancing
Implement auto-scaling groups to replace failed instances automatically
Regular automated backups with tested restore procedures
Implement health checks to detect and replace unhealthy instances
Plan for instance type retirement and migration to newer generations
Consider reserved instances for cost optimisation of steady-state workloads
costConsiderations: VM costs are incurred 24/7 regardless of utilisation — right-size instances
Reserved instances or savings plans reduce costs for predictable workloads
OS licensing costs (Windows Server) add significant per-instance expense
Operational costs for patching, monitoring, and incident response are higher than managed services
Storage costs for VM disks, snapshots, and backups
Consider the total cost of ownership including staff time for VM management
operationalConsiderations: Regular OS patching cycles required — plan maintenance windows
Capacity planning needed for VM instance sizing and scaling
Incident response procedures for VM-level failures and security events
Log collection and centralisation from multiple VM instances
End-of-life planning for OS versions and commercial software support

questionsToAsk: Why can't this workload be containerised or run on a managed platform service?
What OS and software licensing constraints exist?
Is this a temporary lift-and-shift or a long-term hosting model?
What is the patching and maintenance window strategy?
Who will be responsible for ongoing VM management and security hardening?
Is there a modernisation roadmap to move away from VM-based hosting?
commonMistakes: Treating cloud VMs like on-premises servers — not leveraging cloud-native features
Not implementing automated patching, leaving VMs vulnerable to known exploits
Over-sizing VM instances without monitoring actual resource utilisation
Not planning a modernisation path, perpetuating legacy patterns indefinitely
Managing VMs manually instead of using infrastructure-as-code and automation
